title: Question 5

parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
On Fig. 5.2, sketch the variation of the frequency of sound heard by the observer with time $t$, from time $t = 0$ to $t = t_2$.

{{figure:figure_5_2}}

markscheme_points.text: sketch: approximately horizontal line above horizontal dashed line from $t = 0$ to $t = t_1$ and approximately horizontal line below horizontal dashed line from $t = t_1$ to $t = t_2$

hints: Hint 1: Think about how the motion of the train changes the wavelength arriving at the observer before $t_1$ when it is approaching, compared to after $t_1$ when it is moving away, while its speed stays constant.
parts.proper_answer: Constant observed frequency greater than $f_S$ from $t=0$ to $t=t_1$, then a sudden drop at $t_1$ to a constant observed frequency less than $f_S$ from $t=t_1$ to $t=t_2$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture the Doppler shift**
You are standing still and the source is moving at constant speed. When the train moves towards you, each new wave crest is emitted from a point closer to you, so the waves get squashed together. Shorter observed wavelength means higher observed frequency, and because the speed is constant this higher frequency stays constant.

Step 2: **What happens at the passing point**
At $t = t_1$ the train passes you. It changes instantly from approaching to receding. When receding, each new crest is emitted from further away, so the waves are stretched out. Longer observed wavelength means lower observed frequency, again constant because speed is constant. So draw two flat lines with a sudden step down at $t_1$, the first above the $f_S$ dashed line, the second below it.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
At a particular time, the sound waves at the observer have an intensity of $4.7 \times 10^{-3}\text{ W m}^{-2}$. The waves at the observer are incident at right angles on a circular detector of radius $2.8\text{ cm}$.

Calculate the power $P$ of the waves incident on the detector.
hints: Hint 1: Start from what intensity means physically - power spread over an area - and rearrange to make power the subject.
Hint 2: Work out the area that actually collects the power, remembering the detector is circular and the radius needs to be in metres for SI consistency.
Hint 3: Multiply your intensity by your area in SI units and check the power of ten and that the final unit is $\text{W}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link intensity to power**
Intensity $I$ tells you how much power $P$ passes through each square metre at right angles to the wave. That is: $$I = \frac{P}{A}$$ where $A$ is the area intercepting the waves. Rearranged for power: $$P = I \times A$$

Step 2: **Find the detector area in SI units**
The detector is a circle of radius $r = 2.8 \text{ cm} = 0.028 \text{ m}$. Its area is: $$A = \pi r^2 = \pi \times (0.028)^2$$ $$A \approx 2.46 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}^2$$ A common slip is to leave $r$ in cm, which gives an area 10000 times too large.

Step 3: **Calculate the incident power**
Now multiply by the given intensity $I = 4.7 \times 10^{-3} \text{ W m}^{-2}$: $$P = (4.7 \times 10^{-3}) \times (2.46 \times 10^{-3})$$ $$P \approx 1.2 \times 10^{-5} \text{ W}$$ This tiny power makes sense because the detector area is only a few thousandths of a square metre.
